That line is mine, from the direction page, and it's shorthand that nobody could read. Here is what it means.

**The two names.** In the interpreter's library, a 64-bit float is declared twice:

```
trait RR64 ... comprises { Float }
value object Float extends RR64
```

`comprises { Float }` says that every `RR64` value is a `Float`, and that nothing else may extend `RR64`. So `RR64` is the name that programs write, and `Float` is the object that every value really is. `Float` is the "second name". Four more types have one: `ZZ32` with `Int`, `ZZ64` with `Long`, `ZZ` with `BigNum`, `NN64` with `UnsignedLong`. `NN32` and `RR32` have only one name. Each is written `value object NN32` directly.

**"Closed".** A type is closed when no program can add a new kind of value below it. The interpreter's library closes `RR64` with that `comprises` clause. The compiler's own library does not. There `trait RR64` is open, so a program may write `object MyFloat extends RR64`.

**Why a bare `double` needs it.** You said on 11-13 that the compiled path must do better than an object around every number. For that, compiled code holds `x: RR64` as a JVM `double`. It can only do so if every `RR64` value is the same one thing. If a program can add its own kind of `RR64`, a `double` cannot hold it.

**"Merged away".** Write `value object RR64` directly, as `NN32` already is, and delete `Float`, `Int`, `Long`, `BigNum` and `UnsignedLong`. A probe did this in a scratch tree on 11-13. All but one of the interpreter's 830 tests passed, and the one that failed is a test that expects a failure. Both microGPT quick checks passed.

**What is yours to decide.** After the switch-over there is one library, so one shape of the number types has to stand: open, closed with two names, or closed with one. 4. Where nothing fixes a type, the default: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by value, and `RR64`. Both paths alike.
5. An expression of literals alone folds exactly; `1/10` is an exact `QQ` through integer division.
6. `SEQV` and `=` go by the value, whatever the digits or base; string literals of one text are one object.
7. The float tie rule reads `RR64`.

**What this settles:** your three surprises, the `Int` leak, the 24 glue bindings, the exactness for the interval and decimal cases, and one sentence for the specification in place of the Draft's unfinished numeral types.

**What is still open:**
- Your word on B itself, and on the hybrid (point 3) beside it. Nothing about B changes with the hybrid; it adds point 3.
- Whether `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` may be written by a program at all, or only as a coercion's parameter type.
- The bend of the team's print test, which prints a 32-digit numeral as written.

**What the prototype covers:** B's compiled side, built and measured; the three user-type cases, built; the hybrid, costed by reading. I've just sent it the last pieces, by reading only: the literal types' accessors for the four parameters, and the three tests that decide the hybrid, the round trip, the decimal type and equivalence by value across bases. Not in it: walk's side, whose rungs the earlier probes sized.

So nothing more needs prototyping before you decide. When the report lands I give yo …[cut 121]

The exploration found that a wipe is never the fix: a stale result means the edited component was not recompiled.
      03dbb4bf| 
      03dbb4bf| With seeding: a worktree starts as a copy of the base build, its compiled classes and its caches with their path keys translated, so it begins warm. After a .fss edit the worker recompiles that component alone. After a Java or Scala edit it runs ant compileAll, which deletes default_repository/caches itself (build.xml's cleanCache), then restores global.map and recompiles the library in order before the next compiled run. The build's own deletion is the only one; nobody deletes the caches by hand.

The linker throws "Cannot find global.map" when the file is missing, and cleanCache deletes it, hence the restore. The cleaner fix would be to stop tracking it and have the build write the empty map. === 2026-09-08T22:10:20.628Z L2754 assistant
Fortress has them, in the specification, and the implementation ignores them. That is the whole story in one line, and it is a good example of the pattern.

**In the spec.** An object is either a value object or a reference object. A value object has only immutable fields, has no identity, and is compared by contents. The modifier is the keyword `value` on the declaration. The built-in numbers are declared this way: `value object Float extends RR64`, `value object Int extends ZZ32`, `value object Boolean`, and the library uses it for `Just`/`Nothing` and the like. Semantically this is Swift's struct: copied freely, no identity, no mutation.

**In the implementation.** The code generator has no special handling for value objects. A `value object` is compiled to the same heap class as a reference object, allocated and pointed at like everything else. The property the spec grants, that copying a value object is unobservable, is exactly the licence a compiler needs to keep it in registers or flatten it into an array, and the 2012 compiler never used it. The JVM offered no way to express a flat value in 2012, so the modifier stayed a type-checking fact.

**Neighbours.**

- **Java records** are not value classes. A record is a concise heap object with identity. It gives you a constructor, accessors and equality, and still allocates.
- **Valhalla value classes** are the JVM finally adding what Fortress specified: identity-free classes the VM may flatten into arrays and registers. Wh …[cut 1013]

**The two layouts.** Take `value object Point(x: RR64, y: RR64)` and an array of a thousand of them.

The second layout needs nothing from the VM. It is a compiler decision. And for numeric code it is often the better layout anyway: a loop over all the `x`s reads one contiguous array, which is what SIMD wants, and it is how NumPy and JAX lay out fields internally. The game-engine world calls this data-oriented design.

A Kotlin data class has identity: two equal-looking instances are distinguishable by reference comparison, and a field can be mutated through one reference and observed through another. **How wrong are you? Not wrong.** You have re-derived the mainstream design. Karpathy hangs the graph on each scalar because micrograd is a teaching device. Every real framework hangs the graph on tensors and keeps the elements plain floats. Papers state backprop at the matrix level anyway, for example ∂L/∂W = δ xᵀ, so a matrix-level graph is arguably closer to the literature than the scalar one.

Three ways to move the graph off the number:

1. **Tape.** Values are plain library `Vector`/`Matrix` over `RR64`. Each differentiable op computes forward with library arithmetic and pushes a backward closure onto a tape. Something must still name the tensor, so a thin handle wrapping the library matrix plus a node id remains. Custom type at the tensor level, none at the element level.
2. **Expression tree.** The forward pass builds a tree of nodes such as MatMul, Softmax, RMSNorm. A `grad` walk over the tree in reverse produces cotangents. The tree is data, the values are plain matrices. This is your "tree of computations" literally.
3. **Functional backprop.** Each op returns a pair, the value and a linear map from output cotangent to input cotangent. Composition is the chain rule. No tape, no identity, no mutation. Sharing in the DAG, the residual stream and weights reused per position, is handled by summing cotangents where a value fans out.

- The other way out would be to drop Number from those bounds and keep only the algebra, which is a redesign of the library's own declarations. The review did not propose it, and the team's prelude did not do it.

- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). That edge case you are asking me about, I believe we discussed this with the coordinator last night. Can you check it there? I believe, like, I answered it already.

=== 2026-11-09T16:36:16.549Z L7233 assistant
Checked. You did answer it, at 23:10 to 23:23 on 11-08.

- 23:10 (L5019): "Doesn't the natural numeral imply there is no sign, that it's only positive numbers".
- 23:11, the coordinator (L5022): `-3` "is the prefix operator `-` applied to the numeral `3`"; with the fold, "`-3`, `3 + 4` and `1/2` become one exact signed value before anything else"; "`-2147483648` ... Folding first gives the exact value, which fits `ZZ32`"; for a program's own type, "`c: CC64 = -3` is `-(3)`: the coercion receives the numeral `3` with its four numbers, and the type's own prefix `-` applies to the result. A type that cannot be negated refuses it."
- 23:22, the judgement's repair 3 (L5088): "The fold yields a signed constant ... an integer result defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient as `QQ`, a result with a radix point as `RR64`. This is what makes `x = 7/2` a `QQ` and `-2147483648` a `ZZ32` ... A program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only."
- 23:23 (L5096): "Yeah. Option one."

So the sign and `-2147483648` are settled as the design says: fold first, exactly; at a built-in type the folded value converts; at your own type the coercion gets the written numeral and the type's own `-` applies after.

The one part of edge case 2 the words leave implicit is `2 + 3` or `1/2` at your own type. Repair 3's last sentence, "a written numeral only", gives one reading: only a written numeral goes through the numeral coercion; `2 + 3` is two numerals defaulting to `ZZ32` and adding, and `1/2` is a `QQ`, so your type takes them only if it declares a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`, and refuses them otherwise, since coercions do not chain. That is the simple reading, and it matches what you took. I'll put it in the snapshot as the reading of repair 3 unless you say otherwise.

Edge case 3: the `=` pairs between a numeral and a number type, eleven each way as built. When every numeral converts at compile time, is any pair needed? My reading: none; `5 = n` folds `5` to `n`'s type before `=` is chosen, as `1/2 = 0.5` already folds.
